query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In rare‐earth‐free HEAs for magnetic refrigeration, adding a small amount of an FCC metal (e.g., Cu) combined with optimized annealing reduces the spread of local exchange interactions, thereby homogenizing the magnetic phase transition at low applied fields. This enhanced magnetic uniformity sharpens the magnetocaloric response and minimizes hysteresis while preserving a microstructure that facilitates rapid heat exchange and maintains mechanical stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A NiFeCoCr‐based high-entropy alloy that inherently displays a broad distribution of magnetic exchange energies and defects from processing (e.g., as-rolled state).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low-percentage substitution of an FCC metal such as Cu (or a similar cost‐effective element) into the HEA, followed by a tailored annealing heat treatment to promote chemical and structural homogenization.
generation.conditions: Testing under operating temperatures near room temperature (or the target refrigeration temperature range) and at low applied magnetic fields (~1 T), while maintaining a single-phase solid solution.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced structural coherence and reduced defect density that narrows the distribution of interatomic exchange interactions, leading to a more uniform magnetic microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The FCC additive promotes ordering at a local scale, thereby reducing local magnetic anisotropy variations and defect-induced inhomogeneities. This results in a sharper, nearly second-order magnetic phase transition with lower magnetic hysteresis. Simultaneously, the improved microstructural coherence maintains high thermal conductivity and mechanical integrity, essential for rapid heat exchange and operational stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy without the additive, the modified HEA will exhibit a higher magnetic entropy change per field increment, a more pronounced and narrower ΔS peak (indicative of a sharper phase transition), reduced hysteresis in magnetization loops, and retained mechanical stability with faster thermal response.
generation.baseline: The pure NiFeCoCr-based HEA (e.g., in its as-rolled or non-optimized state) that exhibits broader magnetic transition characteristics, higher hysteresis, and less effective heat transfer due to inhomogeneous local exchange interactions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for single-phase, densely packed HEAs (FCC or BCC) used in magnetic refrigeration applications operating near room temperature and under low applied fields (~1 T). It may not apply if secondary phases develop or if the additive concentration deviates significantly from the controlled low-percentage range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in magnetic entropy change, hysteresis reduction, and thermal conductivity are uncertain and will likely depend on the precise additive concentration, heat treatment parameters, and the inherent alloy composition. Further exploration is needed to optimize these variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy sets: one baseline NiFeCoCr-based HEA and one with 3–5 atomic% Cu substitution. Both sets should be processed under identical conditions, with the Cu-containing samples receiving an optimized annealing treatment. Measure the magnetocaloric effect (ΔS vs. temperature) at low applied fields (~1 T), characterize the magnetic hysteresis via magnetization loops, and assess the thermal conductivity and mechanical properties.
measurements: Magnetization as a function of temperature and field to extract the magnetic entropy change (ΔS) and determine the peak sharpness.
Hysteresis loop measurements to quantify coercivity and energy losses.
Thermal conductivity tests to evaluate heat exchange rates.
Mechanical property assessments (e.g., hardness, tensile strength) to verify structural stability.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-substituted and annealed HEA does not exhibit a statistically significant sharpening of the ΔS peak at low fields, reduced hysteresis, and equal or improved thermal conductivity and mechanical stability compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Delving deeper, unfortunately, RCP tends to overestimate the merits of the materials which have a large temperature range of magnetocaloric effect (δTFWHM) but small entropy changes [,] in no small part because materials with same relative cooling power can behave differently in a magnetic cooling simulation []. Moreover, one of the last printed books about magnetic cooling ignores this figure of merit []. In order to be of use in magnetic refrigeration applications the chosen materials have to show a large magnetocaloric effect—a large magnetic entropy change. Besides this, there is a list of requirements related with heat transfer, heat capacity, heat conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, hysteresis losses, eddy currents losses, etc. Therefore, magnetic measurements can be a trusted guide in deciding if a material deserves the effort of complete characterization. Some compounds of the type A1−xBxMnO3 can be considered to be of interest for magnetic refrigeration because some of these compounds show −ΔSm values (−ΔSm ≈ 4–6 J·kg−1·K−1 for ΔH = 5 T) comparable to intermetallic alloys []. This is the case of our investigated compounds.

The calculations indicate that (RuNiFeMoCr)3O4 exhibits a Ru-site distribution more favorable for forming homogeneous local environments, which is thermodynamically consistent with the observed trend of enhanced structural stability (figs. S26 to S28). Electronic structure analysis and free energy calculations compared the (RuNiFeMoCr)3O4 (311) surface with the RuO2 (110) surface (Fig. 5A) (). It should be noted that the calculations in this section are based on representative SQS configurations and idealized static surfaces to extract comparable relative trends, without explicitly accounting for possible surface reconstruction/segregation, dynamic valence-state changes, or electrolyte/potential effects under acidic OER conditions. Changes in −ΔSmax as well as the changes in the shape of the −ΔS(ΔH, T) curves are important to MCE when applied to magnetic refrigeration, as they may lead to changes in the overall refrigerant capacity (RC). RC in general is the figure of merit used to compare MCE materials giving the total heat transfer of the material over a typical refrigeration cycle. RC for a given ΔH is calculated as the integral of −ΔS(T) over a temperature range of interest: Here, TR1 and TR2 are traditionally taken to be the temperatures corresponding to the FWHM of the −ΔS(T) feature on the low and high temperature sides of the peak, respectively. We do not consider hysteretic losses here, as the M(H) loops showed negligible hysteresis, though that can be important in many systems. Figure 5 shows RC as a function of ΔH for both the annealed and as-rolled samples. The RC of 36 J/kg for a 1 T field change puts these HEAs below many other materials designed to operate in the 100–200 K range, though several factors related to pragmatic engineering issues (e.g., ductility, corrosion resistance, high thermal conductivity) may make up for this.
